list.listitem: Most hiccups are of the benign self-limiting type lasting less than 24 hours, and these require no investigation. C
Consider respiratory maneuvers for the initial treatment of non-persistent hiccups. C
There is insufficient evidence supporting the efficacy and safety of pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic therapies for persistent (>48 hours) and intractable (>1 month) hiccups in adults. B
Patients with persistent (>48 hours) or intractable (>1 month) hiccups should be evaluated for systemic disease, including underlying malignancy. C
No single agent is considered the treatment of choice for hiccups. Chlorpromazine is the only FDA-approved medication, but baclofen and metoclopramide are also commonly used. C

background.definition: Hiccups are caused by a sudden, involuntary, spasmotic contraction of the diaphragm and inspiratory intercoastal muscles terminated by abrupt closure of the glottis stopping the inflow of air and producing the characteristic sound. Hiccups usually occur with a frequency of 4 to 60 a minute. The medical term for hiccup is singultus, from the Latin singult, meaning the act of catching one's breath while sobbing. Hiccups are usually classified as benign self-limiting (<24 hours), chronic (24 hours to 1 month), or intractable (>1 month).

list.listitem: Self-limited hiccups are extremely common and occur randomly.
Intractable hiccups (lasting >1 month) occur in approximately 1 in 100,000 persons a year.
Benign hiccups occur equally in males and females, but there is a 4 to 1 male to female ratio for chronic/intractable hiccups.
In men over 90% of chronic/intractable hiccups have an organic cause, while in women most are of psychogenic cause.

Vagus and phrenic nerve irritation: tumors, pericarditis, eventration, splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, hepatitis, peritonitis, pancreatitis, pseudocysts, pharyngitis, laryngitis, pneumonia, aortic aneurysm, tuberculosis, myocardial infarction, lung cancer, esophageal lesions, achalasia, Candida esophagitis, obstruction, gastric lesions, inferior vena cava stening, or carcinoma.
Central nervous system disorders: brain stem tumors, vascular lesions, Parkinson's disease, or foreign object irritating tympanic membrane.
Toxic-metabolic disorders: alcoholism, uremia, hyponatremia, gout, chemotherapy, or diabetes.
Drug induced: dexamethasone, methylprednisolone, sertraline, antipsychotics, anabolic steroids (megastrol acetate in particular), benzodiazepines, or alpha methyldopa.
Hiccups associated with dexamethasone use is associated with male gender, young age, and obesity.
Psychogenic disorders: hysterical neurosis, grief, or malingering.
Hiccups result from stimulation of one or more limbs of the hiccup reflex arc with a "hiccup center" located in the upper spinal cord.

The hiccup reflex arc is composed of three parts: (1) the afferent limb—phrenic and vagus nerves and the sympathetic chains, (2) a central mediator, and (3) the efferent limb—phrenic nerve with accessory efferent neural connections to the glottis and inspiratory intercostal muscles.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Irritation of the vagus nerve branches

list.listitem: Benign self-limiting hiccups lasting less than 24 hours require no diagnostic procedures. C

Persistent (>48 hours) or intractable (>1 month) hiccups may signal an underlying malignancy or other serious condition such as uremia, electrolyte abnormalities, multiple sclerosis, pericarditis, thoracic or abdominal aneurysms, or inflammatory bowel disease. C
Workup for malignancy or other serious medical disease should begin once hiccups have been present for longer than one month. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Presence of a pacemaker dysfuction upon ECG tracing or interrogation

list.listitem: A detailed history and physical is not needed for patients with benign acute hiccups.
In patients with chronic or intractable hiccups, take a history of any comorbidities, any signs or symptoms of malignancy, and alcohol or drug use.
Pertinent findings from the cardiopulmonary exam may include dullness on percussion of the lung fields (mass or pleural effusion) or a pericardial rub with chest auscultation (pericarditis).
Palpation of the abdomen may reveal splenomegaly or hepatomegaly.
An abnormal cranial nerve exam may indicate the presence of a brain stem lesion, while a tremor or shuffling gait may indicate Parkinson's disease.
No specific diagnostic tests are indicated for benign hiccups lasting less than 24 hours.
Chronic or intractable hiccups require a laboratory and radiographic investigation guided by the history and physical.
Labs tests to consider include CBC (anemia or thrombocytosis due to underlying malignancy), serum creatinine and electrolytes (uremia and renal disease), and LFTs (liver disease).
Order an ECG in patients with chest pain to rule out pericarditis.
An MRI of the brain may confirm a brain stem lesion, a CT of the chest may confirm a lung mass or sub-diagphragmatic abscess, and a lumbar puncture may confirm the presence of carcinomatosis.
An EGD can identify an esophageal obstruction, infection or evidence of GERD, and esophageal manometry is useful in documenting the presence of GERD.
PFTs may document laryngeal obstruction, and bronchoscopy can help diagnose the cause of a suspected mass seen on CT or CXR.
In patients with chronic or intractable hiccups, ask about comorbidities, and alcohol and drug use.
Labs to consider as part of the initial evaluation include CBC, serum creatinine, electrolytes, and chest radiograph.
Other studies to consider based on the individual history and physical may include LFTs, ECG, MRI of head, chest CT, lumbar puncture, endoscopy, esophageal manometry, PFTs, bronchoscopy, or EEG.

The initial treatment of hiccups involves respiratory maneuvers such as breath holding, rebreathing into a bag, compression of the diaphragm, ice application in the mouth, or induction of sneeze or cough. C
There is insufficient evidence supporting the efficacy and safety of pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic therapies for persistent (>48 hours) and intractable (>1 month) hiccups in adults. B
Consider treating hiccups lasting more than 24 hours with chlorpromazine, metoclopramide, baclofen,gabapentin, or valproic acid. C

In cases refractory to medical therapy, diaphragmatic irritation from anesthetic phrenic and cervical blocks may be effective. Other options for intractable hiccups include vagal stimulation with ocular compression, carotid massage, or digital rectal massage. B

Although not FDA approved for this indication, baclofen (5-10 mg tid) is the preferred initial pharmacologic agent due to a better safety profile than other agents. It was shown to be effective in a double-blinded randomized crossover trial of four patients with intractable hiccups. Baclofen is thought to act by increasing the threshold for excitation, causing depression of synaptic transmission in the spinal cord. Adverse reactions include drowsiness (63%), asthenia, confusion, dizziness, fatigue, headache, and, rarely, seizure. Other common non-CNS side effects include nausea and emesis, increased urinary frequency, pruritus, and urticaria.

An alternative that is FDA-approved is chlorpromazine (25-50 mg IV or po). The mechanism for terminating hiccups is unknown. Adverse reactions to chlorpromazine include hypotension, dystonia, and drowsiness.

Other potential treatments based only on case reports or case series include haloperidol (2-12 mg IM), phenytoin (200 mg IV, then 100 mg qid), metoclopramide (5-10 mg qid), nifedipine (10-20 mg 1-3 times a day), amitriptyline (10 mg tid), lidocaine (1.5 mg/kg IV infusion, then 0.75 mg/kg a day), and gabapentin (up to 1800 mg/d in divided doses). Methylcellulose (3 sachets in 300 ml warm water) was apparently successful in 2 cases.

Amantadine and/or carbidopa-levopopa may be successful for hiccups associated with Parkinson's disease. Nefopam (a nonopioid analgesic with anti-shivering properties related to antihistamines and antiparkinsonian drugs) is available outside the United States in IV and oral forms.
In cases refractory to medications, consider a phrenic nerve block or electrical stimulation of the dominant hemidiaphragm.
Other potentially useful procedures include dilation of a esophageal stricture or obstruction and catheter stimulation of the pharynx for operative and postoperative hiccups.
One small case series reported success in 3 patients with persistent post-operative hiccups (3-6 days) using a stellate ganglion block.
Evidence from case reports support the use of hypnosis and acupuncture, but no randomized controlled trials have been published.

Household remedies without published evidence abound, including swallowing a spoonful of sugar or peanut butter, sucking on a hard candy, holding breath while increasing pressure on the diaphragm (Valsalva maneuver), tongue traction, and lifting the uvula with a cold spoon.
Other suggested remedies include drinking from the far side of a glass, inducing fright, using smelling salts, rebreathing into a paper bag (do not use plastic), and sipping ice water.
Digital rectal massage has been reported to be effective.
Most hiccups are of the benign self-limiting type lasting less than 24 hours. The long-term prognosis is excellent. C
Persistent and intractable hiccups may be symptoms of many systematic diseases, including malignancy. C
Hiccups frequently cease during sleep.
Most acute benign hiccups spontaneously resolve or resolve with home remedies.
Intractable hiccups may last for years to decades.
Hiccups may persist despite bilateral phrenic nerve transection.
Fetal hiccups are noted by rhythmic fetal movements.
Fetal hiccups frequently recur in subsequent pregnancies, but they have no known physiologic function.
